value: in Y-tube olfactometer bioassays only four of seven EAG-active synthetic plant volatiles (m-xylene, butyl acrylate, butyl propionate, butyl butyrate) elicited positive behavioural responses from adults
units: categorical (Y-tube choice versus mineral-oil solvent, chi-squared goodness-of-fit)

source.authors: Hongsheng Pan, Yanhui Lu, Chunli Xiu, Huihui Geng, Xiaoming Cai, Xiaoling Sun, Yongjun Zhang, Livy Williams III, Kris A. G. Wyckhuys, Kongming Wu
source.title: Volatile fragrances associated with flowers mediate host plant alternation of a polyphagous mirid bug

method: behavioural: single-insect Y-tube olfactometer; each synthetic compound (10 ul of a 1 ug/ul dilution, i.e. 10 ug, on a 5 x 0.5 cm filter paper) against mineral oil solvent; 60 adults per gender per compound
conditions: Unmated 6 to 8 day old adults, from bugs collected in cotton fields at Langfang (Hebei, China) and reared on green bean pods and 10 % sucrose. Seven compounds were EAG-active in flowering-plant headspace (EAG on 10 individuals per sex per compound). Y-tube results by sex: m-xylene female P = 0.036, male P = 0.039; butyl acrylate female P = 0.003, male P = 0.010; butyl propionate female P = 0.014, male P = 0.022; butyl butyrate female P = 0.001, male P = 0.002. Results: no difference between genders for any of the seven compounds (P > 0.05). The three other EAG-active compounds, (Z)-3-hexen-1-ol, (Z)-3-hexenyl acetate and 3-ethylbenzaldehyde, were not attractive in the Y-tube; the Results text gives no statistics or percentages for them. Bioassays ran 08:00 to 18:00 h after 4 h starvation; each insect was used once, with fresh filter paper, and the Y-tube was replaced with a clean one after every four insects. Individuals that remained unresponsive were not included in the analysis and their number is not reported, so the test is of responders. The paper does not say whether Y-tube arms were swapped or assigned at random. Not a sensitivity measure: single dose, no detection threshold or non-detection disclosure. Same paper: in greenhouse cages and field bucket traps the four compounds caught more bugs than solvent controls.
quote: Although the adults responded to all seven synthetic plant volatiles in electroantennography tests, only four (m-xylene, butyl acrylate, butyl propionate and butyl butyrate) elicited positive behavioral responses in Y-tube olfactometer bioassays.
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces and both neighbouring sentences seen, so both ends are verified. Family and order from the paper's Abstract and Introduction ('Hemiptera: Miridae'). The page also gave the P values in Results (Behavioral responses of A. lucorum adults to synthetic volatiles). value: male and female adults showed positive chemotaxis in Y-tube tests toward volatiles from Cinnamomum camphora
units: categorical (Y-tube response rate versus air control, chi-squared)

source.authors: Cong Chen, Zhaoyan Lin, Jingyi Du, Jingyi Huang, Chunmei Ling, Jianfeng Chen
source.title: Olfactory Selection Preferences of Pagiophloeus tsushimanus (Coleoptera: Curculionidae) Adults Toward Lauraceae Plants

method: behavioural: glass Y-tube olfactometer (4 cm inner diameter, 20 cm arms at 60 degrees, 40 cm main arm, 300 mL/min airflow); five two-year-old twigs of about 10 cm per arm against an empty-bottle air control; three repetitions of 12 adults (6 female, 6 male) per comparison; arms reversed after each test
conditions: Results section 3.3.1 against air: C. camphora attracted females (chi2 = 5.974, p < 0.01) and males (chi2 = 4.010, p < 0.05); females did not respond to C. chekiangensis (chi2 = 0.724) or P. chekiangensis (chi2 = 1.290) twigs (both p > 0.05). Larvae and pupae collected from 15-year-old camphor trees in southern China (sites and dates not given) and reared in the laboratory; adults emerging on the same day were selected and starved 24 h. Insects that did not enter the marked area within 5 min were recorded as no-choice and not used for calculation; their number is not reported, so response rates are of responders. Tested at 2000 lx, 26 +/- 1 C; time of day not stated; arm reversal described but no randomisation procedure. Same Results section 3.3.1: males responded significantly less to C. chekiangensis and P. chekiangensis twigs than to air (the male chi2 is printed as 4.010 for both, which looks like a reporting error), and plant-versus-plant tests preferred C. camphora over both (e.g. females v C. chekiangensis chi2 = 11.227) with C. chekiangensis against P. chekiangensis null (females chi2 = 0.502, males chi2 = 0.020); no sex differences were significant. The Abstract sentence quoted also says both sexes had a negative chemotaxis to C. chekiangensis and P. chekiangensis; the Results support that for males only (females null, above), so the value carries only the C. camphora clause (audit 357). Selection coefficients (Table 1, female then male): C. camphora 0.363 +/- 0.104 and 0.306 +/- 0.028; C. chekiangensis -0.131 +/- 0.072 and -0.306 +/- 0.028; P. chekiangensis -0.178 +/- 0.097 and -0.310 +/- 0.156; the sexes did not differ (t = 0.535, 2.251, 0.717, all p > 0.05); no test of a coefficient against zero is reported. Single-compound Y-tube tests (section 3.5): linalool attracted both sexes (chi2 = 6.237 and 4.163, p < 0.05), beta-caryophyllene was null (chi2 = 1.147 and 1.029), alpha-phellandrene and trans-nerolidol were avoided by both sexes. Choice and no-choice feeding tests: both sexes fed most on C. camphora, with C. chekiangensis and P. chekiangensis not differing from each other. Odour preference at one distance, not a detection threshold.
quote: The Y-shaped olfactometer experiments and electroantennography measurements results showed that male and female adults of P. tsushimanus had a positive chemotaxis towards volatiles released by C. camphora and a negative chemotaxis towards volatiles released by C. chekiangensis or P. chekiangensis.
note: Sentence read whole in three abutting pieces (start and end seen); the chi-squared figures in conditions come from Results section 3.3.1, read in pieces, and are not part of the quote. Family and order from the paper (title and Taxonomy line: Coleoptera: Curculionidae). Pagiophloeus tsushimanus was described by Morimoto 1982 (Esakia 19: 51-121, 10.5109/2423, per the BioNames index); no synonym found; not in gbif-names.tsv (audit 357). value: laboratory-reared mosquitoes consistently preferred UV light at 50 to 1000 uW/cm2 over darkness, but did not show a significant preference between darkness and UV light at 1500 uW/cm2
units: categorical (UV versus dark choice by irradiance, uW/cm2)

source.authors: Xinyi Liu, Guoqiang Zhao, Hui Liu, Yuxuan Mao, Meng Xu, Jing Wu, Lijiao Li, Zongzhao Zhai, Pa Wu
source.title: Elimination of Ultraviolet Light-Mediated Attraction Behavior in Culex Mosquitoes via dsRNA-Mediated Knockdown of Opsins

method: behavioural: Y-maze choice between darkness and UV light at graded irradiance
conditions: Y-maze assay: mosquitoes chose between darkness and a UV arm at graded irradiance (5 to 1500 uW/cm2); the UV source alternated between the two long arms across two technical replicates; at least three biological replicates, each with two technical replicates; n per intensity is in supplementary Table S1 and was not read. Females 4 to 10 days after emergence (Figure 1 legend: female mosquitoes); mosquitoes that stayed in the release arm were excluded and their number is not given in the text; Y-maze dimensions, dark adaptation and time of day for the Y-maze are not stated in the text (the video assay was run between ZT6 and ZT12). Wavelength 345 nm is implied by Section 3.1 ('abovementioned experiments'), not stated in the Y-maze Methods; the Y-maze Methods name the meter (UV340B) but not where irradiance was measured, so the irradiance at the mosquito is not established. A further Y-maze test found all three species preferred 395 nm UV over darkness. Laboratory colonies: Cx. quinquefasciatus eggs from the Hunan CDC, Ae. albopictus eggs purchased from Guangzhou Wolbaki Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (commercial supplier; strain and Wolbachia status not stated), Ae. aegypti Liverpool strain (LVP) from a Chinese Academy of Sciences researcher. Preference tested against chance with a one-sample t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test; the Results sentence gives no preference indices or P values (the statistics sit in the Figure 1 legend, not read). Same Section 3.1: Ae. aegypti LVP was more sensitive, preferring 5 to 50 uW/cm2 and showing no significant preference at 150, 500 or 1000 uW/cm2; field-collected Cx. quinquefasciatus preferred UV below 1000 uW/cm2 with no significant phototaxis at 1500 uW/cm2. Silencing four Ae. aegypti opsins left UV attraction unchanged, whereas Cx. quinquefasciatus CqOpsin3, 5 and 6 knockdown (dsGFP injected controls, 1 ug dsRNA per mosquito) reduced or abolished attraction; this record does not use the knockdown results. Preference against darkness only; no other light colour was offered.
quote: Laboratory-reared Cx. quinquefasciatus and Ae. albopictus consistently preferred UV light at intensities ranging from 50 μW/cm2 to 1000 μW/cm2 over darkness, but did not show a significant preference between darkness and UV light at 1500 μW/cm2 …
note: One sentence supports both species lines, each value stated in the clause naming both. Quote read in three abutting pieces with its start (subject) and end seen, and the sentences before and after it; the trailing '([Figure 1]B,C).' is cut and marked. Family and order taken from main for the same species (Culicidae, Diptera; GBIF accepted in gbif-names.tsv). value: preferred body temperature in a laboratory thermal gradient was higher than field body temperature

source.authors: Ana E. Victorica Erostarbe, Franco Valdez Ovallez, José M. Sánchez, Yamila Méndez Osorio, Rodrigo Gómez Alés
source.title: Thermophysiology and Locomotor Performance of the Andean Lizard Phymaturus williamsi: Vulnerable to Rising Temperatures?

method: behavioural: single lizards in a laboratory thermal gradient (terraria of 150 x 45 x 80 cm, linear gradient of 17 to 45 C from infrared lamps of different wattages at varying heights); cloacal ultrafine thermocouples (1 mm) taped in place and logged every 5 min for a 3 h trial during 11:00 to 18:00; mean Tpref per individual, set-point range from the 25 to 75 % interquartile range
conditions: n = 16 wild-caught lizards from Quebrada La Puerta, Calingasta Department, San Juan Province, Argentina (2878 m), caught in October to November 2014 (spring); individually housed at 24 C, trials 3 to 4 days after capture within 8 days of captivity; sex was determined but the sex ratio and any sex effect are not reported (the authors say sex effects cannot be ruled out). Tpref 35.3 C (Figure 2 caption) with a set-point range of 34 to 36.8 C; the mean +/- SD in Table 1 was not read. Field Tb averaged 32.20 +/- 3.24 C in the same season; Tpref was significantly higher than field Tb (Wilcoxon signed-rank T = 16, p < 0.01). Same abstract: thermoregulatory effectiveness E = 0.83; thermal tolerance range 35.41 C; optimal temperatures for locomotor performance were lower than Tpref, so the thermal coadaptation hypothesis was not supported. Exact lamp positions not given. Thermal preference in one gradient, not a thermal sensitivity or detection threshold.
quote: P. williamsi exhibited a preferred temperature higher than field body temperatures, together with high thermoregulatory effectiveness (E = 0.83) and a broad thermal tolerance range (TT = 35.41 °C).
note: Sentence read whole in two abutting pieces, with the preceding and following sentences seen, so both ends are verified; the numbers in conditions come from Results 3.1 and the Figure 2 caption read in pieces. Family and order: Reptile Database page for Phymaturus williamsi Lobo, Laspiur & Acosta, 2013 (Liolaemidae, Squamata, valid current name); the paper itself names Liolaemidae. units: ms (range in which the decision model suggests the behavioural threshold for the inter-leg arrival-time difference lies; model-derived, not a measured threshold)

source.authors: Janez Prešern, Jernej Polajnar, Maarten de Groot, Maja Zorović, Meta Virant-Doberlet
source.title: On the spot: utilization of directional cues in vibrational communication of a stink bug

method: behavioural playback plus recordings: males walked on bean plants to a four-way junction while female calling songs (FCS1 dominant about 83 Hz, FCS2 about 116 Hz) were played to one leaf; laser vibrometer recordings of delay and amplitude on the stalks; leg interneuron recordings with 150 Hz sine stimuli at 0, 0.5 and 1.0 ms delays; a decision model fitted to the measured delay distributions
conditions: Sexually mature bugs 10 to 20 days after the final moult from a laboratory colony at the National Institute of Biology, Ljubljana, derived from one Slovenian population; nothing field-collected for this study. Orientation: 11 males with FCS1 and 19 with FCS2; males started on the apex after 2 min acclimation and the stimulated side was randomised; whether males were reused is not stated. Most males walked first to the vibrated leaf's stalk (FCS1 81 %, N = 11, printed chi2 = 72.02, df = 1, P < 0.01; FCS2 58 %, N = 19, printed chi2 = 42.91, df = 1, P < 0.05); the printed chi-squared values do not look consistent with these sample sizes and are reported as printed. Playback amplitude was only 'adjusted to the level of natural signals', no numeric level at the leaf (the 5 x 10-4 m/s velocity is for the neurophysiology stimuli). Natural delay 0.41 +/- 0.16 ms; amplitude was an unreliable cue (RMS difference 0.16 +/- 0.91 dB, higher on the contralateral stalk in 38 % of recordings; two-dimensional true amplitude difference 1.58 +/- 1.46 dB, 317 of 790 contralateral). Neurophysiology: 42 males, 51 neurons, 11 sensitive to leg delay; a 0.5 ms delay raised latency 6 to 26 % and cut spike count by up to 29 %. Same Abstract sentence: time delays as short as 0.5 ms resulted in marked changes in interneuron activity. Model thresholds: first model 0.27 ms for FCS1 and 0.39 ms for FCS2; second model, which assumes searching males choose randomly among the available directions, 0.31 and 0.46 ms; model inputs were the pooled measured delays and amplitude differences, evaluated at hypothetical thresholds; amplitude-based correct choices never exceeded 35 %. The 0.3 to 0.5 ms figure comes from the decision model, not from a behavioural test of graded delays.
quote: Determined time delays as short as 0.5 ms resulted in marked changes in interneuron activity and the decision model suggests that the behavioural threshold is in the range between 0.3 and 0.5 ms.
note: Sentence read whole in two abutting pieces (start and end seen, as sentence 6 of 6 in the Abstract). Authors: the Nature page truncated the list; Crossref single-DOI lookup gives five authors in the order printed, volume 8, issue 1, article 5418, issued 2018, CC BY 4.0 vor; the page prints only 'Open access' and the copyright line. Family and order from the paper (Hemiptera, Pentatomidae, Abstract). Not on main or any desk branch for sense_vibration (grep of Nezara viridula and the DOI across the whole docs tree; main holds two other sense_vibration rows for the species from different papers (docs/views/audit/corrected/insect.jsonl:425, Virant-Doberlet and Čokl 2004; :427, Zorović 2011; audit 357), not repeats).

value: band-limited vibrational noise impaired males' recognition of the female signal and localisation of its source; overlapping noise decreased receptor-neuron sensitivity to the signal and disrupted frequency encoding, non-overlapping noise only affected frequency encoding
units: categorical (noise masking of a 0.3 mm/s RMS calling song; SNR 6, 0 and -6 dB)

source.authors: Rok Janža, Nataša Stritih-Peljhan, Aleš Škorjanc, Jernej Polajnar, Meta Virant-Doberlet
source.title: Vibrational noise disrupts Nezara viridula communication, irrespective of spectral overlap

method: behavioural playback on bean plants plus leg-nerve recordings: male stink bugs given a female calling song (0.3 mm/s RMS in behaviour, 1 mm/s RMS in physiology) alone (signal-only control) or with band-limited white noise: 50 to 150 Hz (overlapping the fundamental), 50 to 500 Hz (fundamental and harmonics) or 500 to 1000 Hz (non-overlapping), at signal-to-noise ratios of 6, 0 and -6 dB (24 to 0 dB in 6 dB steps in physiology)
conditions: Adult males collected in autumn in coastal Slovenia, hibernated 3 months and isolated for a week before trials. Behaviour: 30 males, each tested under 9 noise treatments plus 1 control over 12 days (25 males per day). Trials were randomised by day and treatment and the playback side was randomised per trial; signal and noise were registered on the stem just below the stem-leaf branching. Physiology: 12 leg-nerve recordings. Because noise reduced participation, continuous comparisons used only control and 6 dB SNR (n = 11 for signalling, n = 20 for searching); Cochran's Q with McNemar post hoc tests, Friedman with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (FDR-corrected), linear mixed models to confirm. Overlapping noise reduced signalling, shortened signalling and lengthened latency most at -6 dB; all noise treatments reduced the percentage of males locating the source with similar effects across bandwidths. Nulls: non-overlapping noise did not reduce the absolute or relative neuronal response to the signal even at higher amplitudes, and the absolute response reduction under overlapping noise was not statistically significant (Wilcoxon, FDR-corrected, p > 0.05); the Abstract's 'decreased sensitivity' refers to the relative response. Exact percentages are in figures and supplementary tables, not read. A reaction to playback of masking noise at measured vibration levels, not a detection threshold or a non-detection test.
quote: Noise impaired the ability of males to recognize the female signal and localise its source: overlapping noise decreased sensitivity of receptor neurons to the signal and disrupted signal frequency encoding by phase-locking units, while non-overlapping noise only affected frequency encoding.
note: Sentence read whole in four abutting pieces; the sentences before and after it were seen, so both ends are verified. Crossref single-DOI lookup: five authors in the order printed (the page truncated the list), volume 7, issue 1, article 1533, issued 2024, CC BY 4.0 vor; the page prints only 'Open access' and the copyright line. Family and order from this paper ('Southern green stink bug Nezara viridula (Hemiptera, Pentatomidae)'; audit 357). Not a repeat of that record: different paper, stimulus and finding.
